name: Proto-Punk
about: Proto-punk is a label applied in hindsight to bands of the mid-1960s and early 1970s whose crudeness, speed and attitude anticipated punk before it had a name. It runs from the garage snarl of The Sonics and The Monks through The Velvet Underground's drone and deadpan to Detroit, where the MC5 and The Stooges turned volume and contempt into a style around 1969, with Iggy Pop as its first frontman. The New York Dolls brought glam trash to Manhattan, the Modern Lovers and Dr. Feelgood stripped rock back to basics, and Death and Rocket from the Tombs recorded punk years before anyone released it. The guitars are overdriven, the drums simple, the singing more a bark than a croon, and the records sold poorly until their disciples made them canon.

artists.name: The Stooges
artists.why: Iggy Pop's band, the essential prototype

artists.name: The Velvet Underground
artists.why: noise, drone and deadpan from New York

artists.name: New York Dolls
artists.why: glam trash that taught punk to dress

artists.name: The Monks
artists.why: American GIs in Germany, 1966, banjo included

artists.name: Dr. Feelgood
artists.why: Canvey Island pub rock at punk tempo

artists.name: Death
artists.why: Detroit's Black punk band, lost until 2009

artists.name: Rocket from the Tombs
artists.why: Cleveland's seedbed for Pere Ubu and Dead Boys

artists.name: The Dictators
artists.why: New York wiseguys who preceded the Ramones

artists.name: Suicide
artists.why: two men, a keyboard and pure confrontation

albums.title: Here Are the Sonics!!!
albums.why: Gerry Roslie's screams and the distorted, overloaded recording of The Witch and Psycho made the rawest American rock record of its decade.

albums.title: My Generation
albums.why: Keith Moon's chaos, Pete Townshend's feedback and the stuttered title song gave British punk a template it never admitted to using.

albums.title: Black Monk Time
albums.why: Five American servicemen in tonsures playing distorted banjo and shouting about Vietnam, a record so strange it took decades to find its audience.

albums.title: From Nowhere
albums.why: Wild Thing and Reg Presley's leering simplicity made the Andover band an unlikely influence on everyone from the Ramones to the MC5.

albums.title: The Velvet Underground & Nico
albums.why: Lou Reed's songs about heroin and sadomasochism over John Cale's drone sold little and, as the saying goes, started a band in everyone who bought it.

albums.title: White Light/White Heat
albums.why: Recorded in the red with Sister Ray's seventeen minutes of distortion, it is the noisiest record a major label released in the 1960s.

albums.title: Kick Out the Jams
albums.why: Recorded live at Detroit's Grande Ballroom, the debut's revolutionary rhetoric and twin-guitar roar made it the loudest political record of its time.

albums.title: The Stooges
albums.why: John Cale produced the Ann Arbor band's debut, where 1969 and I Wanna Be Your Dog reduced rock to a drone, a riff and Iggy's boredom.

albums.title: Fun House
albums.why: Cut almost live with Steve Mackay's saxophone shrieking through L.A. Blues, it is the heaviest and most feral of the proto-punk records.

albums.title: Back in the USA
albums.why: Jon Landau's thin, tight production turned the MC5 into a short-song rock and roll band, and the result sounds like the Ramones six years early.

albums.title: Love It to Death
albums.why: Bob Ezrin's production and I'm Eighteen made the Detroit band's shock-rock into real songs, a bridge between the Stooges and glam.

albums.title: Teenage Head
albums.why: Roy Loney's sleazy San Francisco take on the Stones and rockabilly was reportedly admired by Mick Jagger and ignored by everyone else at the time.

albums.title: Raw Power
albums.why: James Williamson's guitar on Search and Destroy and David Bowie's thin, tinny mix made the record punk's immediate blueprint on both sides of the Atlantic.

albums.title: New York Dolls
albums.why: Johnny Thunders's guitar and David Johansen's camp Jagger routine on Personality Crisis gave punk its look, its attitude and half its chord changes.

albums.title: Too Much Too Soon
albums.why: Shadow Morton's production and too many covers blunted the second album, though Human Being and Puss 'n' Boots keep the trash spirit alive.

albums.title: Down by the Jetty
albums.why: Recorded in mono with Wilko Johnson's stabbing guitar and Lee Brilleaux's menace, the Canvey Island debut is pub rock at punk's speed and intent.

albums.title: Go Girl Crazy!
albums.why: Handsome Dick Manitoba's wrestling-heel persona and Andy Shernoff's songs about TV and fast food made the funniest pre-punk record out of New York.

albums.title: The Modern Lovers
albums.why: Recorded in 1972 with John Cale and shelved for four years, Roadrunner and Pablo Picasso turned Velvets worship into something innocent and wholly new.

albums.title: Suicide
albums.why: Alan Vega's rockabilly hiccup over Martin Rev's buzzing keyboard on Ghost Rider and Frankie Teardrop was more confrontational than any guitar band of the year.

albums.title: (I'm) Stranded
albums.why: Recorded in Brisbane isolation before the band had heard the Ramones, the debut proved punk was arriving independently on three continents.

albums.title: The Day the Earth Met the Rocket from the Tombs
albums.why: The 1975 Cleveland recordings that seeded Pere Ubu and Dead Boys, with the first versions of Sonic Reducer and 30 Seconds Over Tokyo, finally issued properly.

albums.title: ...For the Whole World to See
albums.why: Three brothers from Detroit recorded these seven punk songs in 1975 and were ignored for refusing to change their name; Drag City's release rewrote the timeline.

albums.title: Cyborgs Revisited
albums.why: Hamilton, Ontario's lost 1974 recordings mix Stooges riffs with synthesizer squall, a Canadian proto-punk footnote that deserves better than footnote status.

albums.title: The Seeds
albums.why: Sky Saxon's whine and the two-chord drive of Pushin' Too Hard made Los Angeles garage rock's most punk-sounding debut.
